Thank you for submitting your article "Cell lineage-dependent chiral actomyosin flows drive cellular rearrangements in early development" for consideration by eLife. Your revised manuscript has been seen by the two original reviewers of your manuscript, an additional reviewer who is a senior expert in the field with relevant expertise, a Reviewing Editor and Aleksandra Walczak as the Senior Editor. While all reviewers see potential for an excellent paper, the majority opinion still sees major deficits as outlined below.

The Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

As the editors have judged that your manuscript is of interest, but as described below that additional experiments/analysis/modelling/theory are required before it is published, we would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). First, because many researchers have temporarily lost access to the labs, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts. We are also offering, if you choose, to post the manuscript to bioRxiv (if it is not already there) along with this decision letter and a formal designation that the manuscript is "in revision at eLife". Please let us know if you would like to pursue this option. (If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

Summary:

All reviewers appreciate that the analysis of the P0 cell has been improved and new data using spindle positioning mutants have been added that are consistent with the model. The reviewers agree also that the data generally support the idea that chiral flows can induce spindle rotation (which was known from previous work) and that this study shows that this operates also in other cells, making it a more general phenomenon. It is also appreciated that the manuscript presents a theory that can explain chiral flows.

It remained however unclear to the reviewers how chiral flow around the long axis of the cell produces the tilt in X-Y. Given that so much of the analysis rests on this tilt phenomenon, as indeed does the claim to relevance for development, because the manuscript suggests that this tilt allows ABp-P2 contact, the absence of an attempt to provide a physical explanation for the tilt was considered a critical weakness. The reviewers expect at least some attempt to understand theoretically how the observed tilt can be obtained from the patterns of flow that is observed.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers note that the motion of an elongated objects in a rotational flow is one of the best-studied problems in viscous fluid mechanics and conclude that even with the obvious complexities in the present setup (geometry, non-Newtonian fluids, etc.) it should be possible to make some sensible estimates.

In this context, a particular statement that the reviewers struggled with was "Strikingly, when viewed from either embryo pole, the closest AB-like cell skews clockwise, meaning that the two juxtaposed cells counter- rotate (new, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and new Video 14–16." The reviewers argued that the direction of rotation of both cells in this particular case can be explained by the cell-cell contact area having an increased friction coefficient when compared to the cell- vitelline membrane and/or cell-eggshell contact. Given this topology, the handedness of the chiral flow indeed would be expected to give rise to clockwise rotation of both cells when viewed from the closest pole." This raises the question of whether the cells counter-rotate or both rotate clockwise. The reviewers also note that the observed X-Y tilt of the cells in the same direction has not been addressed here.

Finally, the notion emerged that the manuscript is not particularly reader-friendly, a concern that should be addressed. It is recommended to add a clear schematic early on that explains the geometry more clearly than Figure 1 (or the supplements). Moreover, the terminology "no chiral counter-rotating flows" was found to be confusing. Does that mean that there are chiral flows but they are not counter-rotating, or there are counter-rotating flows but they are not chiral? Indeed, chiral in this sense is not well-explained geometrically (here a schematic could help), especially since the experiments appear to only look at planar projections of the flows.

We would also like to encourage you to include the species studied in the title.

In conclusion, we regret to inform you that your manuscript cannot be accepted in its present form. Because the reviewers see however potential for a manuscript that can be accepted at eLife, they encourage you to address the concerns raised above. In that case, we would be prepared to consider a re-revised version of your manuscript.

claims.claim: Both the presence and the strength of chiral counter-rotating flows are related to the fate of the dividing cell.

claims.claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows are driven by active torque generation that depends on the myosin distribution.

claims.claim: Myosin distributions during division of the AB and the P/EMS-lineage cells differ in specific features.

claims.claim: The early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position.
claims.source: To conclude, the early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position, while early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in these two features.

claims.claim: Early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position.
claims.source: To conclude, the early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position, while early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in these two features.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the measured myosin ratios and ring positions

claims.claim: A symmetric myosin distribution and cytokinetic ring position result in a maximum value of vc.
claims.source: We find that a symmetric myosin distribution and cytokinetic ring position (myosin ratio ≈1, relative myosin peak position ≈0.5) result in a maximum value of vc.
claims.evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling using thin film active chiral fluid theory

claims.claim: Myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc.
claims.source: Accordingly, myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc, where the model suggests that vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claims.claim: vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position.
claims.source: Accordingly, myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc, where the model suggests that vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claims.claim: The switch between chiral and non-chiral flows between the two lineages could in principle be attributed to the observed difference in myosin ratio, cytokinetic ring position or both.
claims.source: Our results indicate that the switch between chiral and non-chiral flows between the two lineages could in principle be attributed to the observed difference in myosin ratio, cytokinetic ring position or both (Appendix 1—table 1).
claims.evidence: Inferred from theoretical modeling and experimental observations

claims.claim: The thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis.
claims.source: We note, however, that while the thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Appendix 1—table 1), this is not possible for the P/EMS lineage.
claims.evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling and comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claims.claim: The thin film active chiral fluid theory cannot quantitatively relate y-direction flows with myosin profiles for the P/EMS lineage.
claims.source: We note, however, that while the thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Appendix 1—table 1), this is not possible for the P/EMS lineage.
claims.evidence: Limitation of the theoretical model when applied to P/EMS lineage

claims.claim: The understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the cortical flows in P/EMS linage divisions is still incomplete.
claims.source: This indicates that our understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the cortical flows in P/EMS linage divisions is still incomplete.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the inability of the theoretical model to explain P/EMS flows

claims.claim: The occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in the cell halves and the position of the cytokinetic ring.
claims.source: Taken together, our analysis implies a mechanism whereby the occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in the cell halves and the position of the cytokinetic ring.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and theoretical modeling

claims.claim: The first cell division in wild-type embryos is asymmetric and does not display chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.source: The first cell division in wild-type embryos is asymmetric and does not display chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claims.claim: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes.
claims.source: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes (Kemphues et al., 1988) and depletion of the posterior Par protein, PAR-2, led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claims.claim: Depletion of PAR-2 led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position.
claims.source: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes (Kemphues et al., 1988) and depletion of the posterior Par protein, PAR-2, led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claims.claim: par-2 depletion triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min).
claims.source: Strikingly, par-2 depletion also triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 9) demonstrating that inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claims.claim: Inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
claims.source: Strikingly, par-2 depletion also triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 9) demonstrating that inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experimental observation that par-2 depletion causes both symmetric division and chiral flows

claims.claim: A centered ring position should result in chiral counter-rotating flows regardless of myosin asymmetry.
claims.source: Moreover, our hydrodynamic theory predicts that a centered ring position should result in chiral counter-rotating flows regardless of myosin asymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: Prediction from theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claims.claim: LIN-5 is involved in generating asymmetric pulling forces that displace the spindle from the center.
claims.source: LIN-5 is involved in generating asymmetric pulling forces that displace the spindle from the center (Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008; Lorson et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claims.claim: The myosin distribution in P0 is still asymmetric in lin-5 (RNAi) embryos, while the ring position is at the center.
claims.source: We first confirmed that indeed the myosin distribution in P0 is still asymmetric in these embryos (albeit reduced when compared with control), while the ring position is at the center (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claims.claim: lin-5 (RNAi) triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −1.73 ± 0.74 µm/min).
claims.source: Quantifying cortical actomyosin flows revealed that lin-5 (RNAi) triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −1.73 ± 0.74 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claims.claim: The emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows upon lin-5 (RNAi) is unlikely to be the result of higher overall actomyosin activity.
claims.source: Given that cortical myosin levels upon lin-5 (RNAi) are comparable to those observed in control, the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows is unlikely to be the result of higher overall actomyosin activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of myosin levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claims.claim: Both asymmetries in myosin distribution and ring position counteract the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.source: Although we cannot fully uncouple the effect of myosin asymmetry and ring position, these experimental results are qualitatively consistent with our theoretical predictions and thus suggest that both, asymmetries in myosin distribution and ring position, counteract the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental results and theoretical predictions

claims.claim: Symmetric cell division is required for chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows to emerge during cytokinesis.
claims.source: We conclude that symmetric cell division is required for chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows to emerge during cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with par-2 and lin-5 perturbations

claims.claim: Specific rotations of the spindle (termed spindle skews) are thought to be a key mechanism by which dividing cells reposition themselves in the embryo.
claims.source: Specific rotations of the spindle (termed spindle skews) are thought to be a key mechanism by which dividing cells reposition themselves in the embryo (Naganathan et al., 2014; Singh and Pohl, 2014; Liro and Rose, 2016; Bergmann et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claims.claim: Cells of the early AB lineage undergo an average skew angle of 21.17 ± 3.22°.
claims.source: We find that cells of the early AB lineage undergo an average skew angle of 21.17 ± 3.22° (AB: 37.51 ± 2.51°, ABa: 27.64 ± 2.29°, ABp: 23.98 ± 1.19°, ABal: 17.73 ± 1.98°, ABar: 15.51 ± 3.51°, ABpl: 10.43 ± 1.92° and ABpr: 15.42 ± 2.11°).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claims.claim: P/EMS lineage cells undergo significantly reduced spindle skews with an average skew angle of 2.32 ± 0.43°.
claims.source: In comparison, P/EMS lineage cells undergo significantly reduced spindle skews with an average skew angle of of 2.32 ± 0.43° (P0: 2.31 ± 1.67°, P1: 2.25 ± 0.66°, EMS: 2.66 ± 1.25°, P2: 4.36 ± 1.67°).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claims.claim: Spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses.
claims.source: Note also, that spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses, while the P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant as development progresses.
claims.source: Note also, that spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses, while the P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: Cells that exhibit significant chiral counter-rotating flows also undergo significant spindle skews during early development.
claims.source: Given that AB lineage cells, but not P/EMS lineage cells, undergo chiral counter-rotating flows, we conclude that cells that exhibit significant chiral counter-rotating flows also undergo significant spindle skews during early development (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Inferred from correlation between flow patterns and spindle skews shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: The skew of the ABa and ABp cells is a three-dimensional process, tilting the spindle in both the anteroposterior-left-right (AP-LR) plane and in the orthogonal left-right-dorsoventral (LR-DV) plane.
claims.source: In our earlier work, we showed that the skew of the ABa and ABp cells is in fact a three-dimensional process, tilting the spindle in both the anteroposterior-left-right (AP-LR) plane and in the orthogonal left-right-dorsoventral (LR-DV) plane (Naganathan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claims.claim: The spindle skew in the AB cell in the AP-DV plane is similar in compressed and uncompressed conditions (37.51 ± 2.51° and 36.67 ± 9.24°, respectively).
claims.source: Chiral counter-rotating flows in the AB cell could still be observed and the spindle skew in the AP-DV plane was similar in compressed and uncompressed conditions (37.51 ± 2.51° and 36.67 ± 9.24°, respectively).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claims.claim: The absence of embryo compression revealed a significant clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane with a skew angle of 31.85 ± 11.11° when viewed from the anterior.
claims.source: However, the absence of embryo compression revealed a significant clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane (when viewed from the anterior) with a skew angle of 31.85 ± 11.11° (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 10).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: No significant skew was observed in the P1 cell in the LR-DV plane.
claims.source: We did not observe any significant skew in the P1 cell in the LR-DV plane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Skews of the AB cell division axis are a three-dimensional process, where the skew occurs in both the AP-DV and LR-DV planes.
claims.source: These findings show that skews of the AB cell division axis are in fact also a three-dimensional process, where the skew occurs in both the AP-DV and LR-DV planes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of skews in both planes

claims.claim: Anteriorizing the embryo via par-2; chin-1; lgl-1 (RNAi) results in the second and the third cell division exhibiting chiral counter-rotating flows with vc values that are not significantly different from one another (−6.53 ± 1.13 µm/min and −6.67 ± 0.8 µm/min, respectively).
claims.source: Consistent with the first expectation, anteriorizing the embryo via par-2; chin-1; lgl-1 (RNAi) (Beatty et al., 2013) results in the second and the third cell division exhibiting chiral counter-rotating flows with vc values that are not significantly different from one another (−6.53 ± 1.13 µm/min and −6.67 ± 0.8 µm/min, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence; Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B,C

claims.claim: Posteriorizing the embryo via par-6 (RNAi) results in both the second and the third cell division not exhibiting counter-rotating flows (vc = 0.07 ± 0.71 µm/min and −0.85 ± 1.13 µm/min, respectively).
claims.source: Consistent with the second expectation, posteriorizing the embryo via par-6 (RNAi) (Hung and Kemphues, 1999) results in both the second and the third cell division not exhibiting counter-rotating flows (vc = 0.07 ± 0.71 µm/min and −0.85 ± 1.13 µm/min, respectively; Figure 3B,C, Videos 11–13).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B,C and Videos 11–13

claims.claim: Cell fate determines the presence or absence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.source: Hence, cell fate determines the presence or absence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments with anteriorizing and posteriorizing perturbations

claims.claim: Switching the cell fate results in concomitant changes in the spindle skew angle in the AP-DV plane for both the second and third cell division in compressed as well as non-compressed embryos.
claims.source: Furthermore, switching the cell fate results in concomitant changes in the spindle skew angle in the AP-DV plane for both the second and third cell division in compressed as well as non-compressed embryos (Figure 3D,H).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3D,H

claims.claim: Spindles of the two AB-like cells in uncompressed anteriorized embryos undergo clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane when viewed from the closest pole (skew angles of each AB-like cell = 26.93 ± 6.78° and 27.44 ± 8.66°).
claims.source: Strikingly, we observed that spindles of the two AB-like cells in uncompressed anteriorized embryos undergo clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane when viewed from the closest pole (skew angles of each AB-like cell = 26.93 ± 6.78° and 27.44 ± 8.66°) (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Videos 14–16).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: Cell fate determines both the presence of chiral counter-rotating flows and the degree as well as the direction of spindle skew.
claims.source: We conclude that cell fate determines both the presence of chiral counter-rotating flows and the degree as well as the direction of spindle skew.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments with cell fate perturbations

claims.claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 results in vc = −3.57 ± 0.57 µm/min, which is reduced in comparison to the unperturbed embryo (vc = −6.6 ± 0.37 µm/min).
claims.source: Weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 results in vc = −3.57 ± 0.57 µm/min, which is reduced in comparison to the unperturbed embryo (vc = −6.6 ± 0.37 µm/min, Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A,B

claims.claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 increases the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity to vc = −8.71 ± 0.58 µm/min.
claims.source: Conversely, weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 increases the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity to vc = −8.71 ± 0.58 µm/min (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A,B

claims.claim: ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations impact only chiral counter-rotating flows, and do not significantly change overall contractility.
claims.source: Note that these perturbations impact only chiral counter-rotating flows, and do not significantly change overall contractility, as illustrated by the on-axis flow into the contractile ring, which is not significantly altered (Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4C

claims.claim: Decreasing the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity by mild ect-2 (RNAi) leads to concomitant reduction of the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 0.59 ± 0.05°/min) as compared to 1.01 ± 0.1°/min in control embryos.
claims.source: We indeed find that decreasing the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity by mild ect-2 (RNAi) leads to concomitant reduction of the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 0.59 ± 0.05°/min, Video 17) as compared to 1.01 ± 0.1°/min in control embryos (Figure 4D, Video 18).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D

claims.claim: Increasing RhoA signaling by mild rga-3 (RNAi) treatment leads to an increase of both the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity and the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 1.29 ± 0.12°/min).
claims.source: Conversely, increasing RhoA signaling by mild rga-3 (RNAi) treatment leads to an increase of both the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity and the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 1.29 ± 0.12°/min (Video 19, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D

claims.claim: The peak rates of spindle elongation remain unchanged as compared to the control for both ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations.
claims.source: Note that the peak rates of spindle elongation remain unchanged as compared to the control for both perturbations (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Changing chiral counter-rotating flow velocities results in concomitant changes of the rates of spindle skews without impacting on the dynamics of spindle elongation.
claims.source: We conclude that changing chiral counter-rotating flow velocities results in concomitant changes of the rates of spindle skews without impacting on the dynamics of spindle elongation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations

claims.claim: Overall actomyosin contractility is unlikely to contribute significantly to cell division skews.
claims.source: In addition, given that the contractility-driven flows remain unaltered upon rga-3 (RNAi) and ect-2 (RNAi), overall actomyosin contractility is unlikely to contribute significantly to cell division skews.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that contractile flows are unchanged while skew rates change

claims.claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows mechanically drive cell skews and consequently also spindle skews.
claims.source: These results instead support our second hypothesis, that chiral counter-rotating flows mechanically drive cell skews and consequently also spindle skews.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations showing correlation between flow velocities and skew rates

claims.claim: The AB cell exhibits chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) upon lin-5 depletion.
claims.source: Moreover, the AB cell exhibited chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) and, although the AB spindle was often misaligned, it skewed substantially during anaphase (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: The AB spindle skewed substantially during anaphase upon lin-5 depletion (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°).
claims.source: Moreover, the AB cell exhibited chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) and, although the AB spindle was often misaligned, it skewed substantially during anaphase (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: The known spindle orientation pathway does not play an important role in driving spindle skews.
claims.source: These results argue against an important role for the known spindle orientation pathway in driving spindle skews.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with lin-5 and gpr-1/2 perturbations

claims.claim: The LIN-5-dependent spindle orientation pathway is known to reorient the metaphase spindle in the P1 cell.

claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claims.claim: Analyzing spindle skews in P1 upon lin-5 (RNAi) and gpr-1/2 (RNAi) revealed no significant difference when compared to control embryos.
claims.source: Analyzing spindle skews in P1 upon lin-5 (RNAi) and gpr-1/2 (RNAi) revealed no significant difference when compared to control embryos, which suggests that the spindle orientation pathway does not overrule actomyosin-dependent spindle skews (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

results.result: Chiral counter-rotating flows arise systematically in early AB lineage cell divisions but not in P/EMS lineage cell divisions. AB lineage cells (AB, ABa, ABp, ABar, ABpr) exhibit significant chiral counter-rotating flow velocities (vc ranging from −7.01 to −1.16 µm/min), while P/EMS lineage cells (P0, P1, EMS, P2) show essentially absent counter-rotating flows (vc ranging from 0.01 to 0.25 µm/min). Instead, P/EMS lineage cells exhibit net-rotating flows where both cell halves move in the same direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C31-C43 provide consistent experimental measurements of flow velocities across multiple cell divisions, with clear quantitative differences between AB and P/EMS lineages. The data shown in Figure 1A-B directly support these measurements, and the distinction between counter-rotating and net-rotating flows is well-documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=5-29 embryos per cell type).

results.result: The chiral counter-rotating flow velocity in the AB lineage decreases as development progresses and cells become smaller, accompanied by a decrease in myosin concentration in the cytokinetic ring. This indicates that both the presence and strength of chiral counter-rotating flows are related to cell fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, demonstrating the correlation between developmental progression, cell size, myosin concentration, and flow velocity. The inference that flow characteristics are related to cell fate (C47) is reasonable given the systematic pattern observed across lineages.

results.result: AB lineage cell divisions are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio (approximately 1.0) and cytokinetic ring position (approximately 0.5 relative to cell length), while P/EMS lineage cell divisions are asymmetric with myosin ratios of 1.67-2.07 and ring positions of 0.57-0.59.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 present quantitative measurements of myosin distribution and ring position with appropriate error estimates. The data shown in Figure 1C-E support these measurements, and the distinction between symmetric (AB lineage) and asymmetric (P/EMS lineage) divisions is clear and well-documented.

results.result: Theoretical modeling using thin film active chiral fluid theory shows that symmetric myosin distribution and centered cytokinetic ring position result in maximum chiral counter-rotating flow velocity, while asymmetries reduce vc. The theory quantitatively recapitulates observed flows in AB lineage cells but not in P/EMS lineage cells, indicating incomplete understanding of P/EMS flow mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 combine theoretical predictions with experimental validation. The thin film active chiral fluid theory successfully predicts AB lineage flows (Figure 1—figure supplement 7-8), but the acknowledged limitation for P/EMS lineage (C62-C63) is appropriately noted. The mechanism proposed in C64 is well-supported by the convergence of theory and experiment.

results.result: PAR-2 depletion converts the asymmetric P0 division into a symmetric division with centered ring position and myosin ratio of one, triggering the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min). This demonstrates that inducing symmetric cell division is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 present a clear genetic perturbation experiment with quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9. The causal relationship between symmetric division and chiral flows (C69) is well-supported by the observation that par-2 depletion simultaneously induces both symmetric myosin distribution and chiral flows.

results.result: LIN-5 depletion results in centered ring position while maintaining myosin asymmetry, triggering chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −1.73 ± 0.74 µm/min). Combined with par-2 results, this suggests that both myosin asymmetry and ring position counteract chiral flow emergence, and symmetric cell division is required for chiral flows.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 present complementary genetic perturbation experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 10) that test theoretical predictions. While the authors acknowledge they cannot fully uncouple myosin asymmetry from ring position effects (C75), the qualitative consistency with theory and the convergent evidence from two different perturbations support the conclusion that symmetric division is required for chiral flows (C76).

results.result: AB lineage cells undergo significant spindle skews (average 21.17 ± 3.22°) that decrease as development progresses, while P/EMS lineage cells show minimal spindle skews (average 2.32 ± 0.43°) that remain constant. Cells exhibiting significant chiral counter-rotating flows also undergo significant spindle skews.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 present systematic measurements of spindle skew angles across multiple cell divisions with appropriate sample sizes. The correlation between chiral flows and spindle skews (C82) is supported by Figure 2B, which shows the relationship between these two parameters across different cell types.

results.result: AB cell division skews occur in three dimensions: the spindle skew in the AP-DV plane is similar in compressed and uncompressed conditions (~37°), but uncompressed embryos reveal an additional significant clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane (31.85 ± 11.11°). No significant skew occurs in the P1 cell in the LR-DV plane.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 present novel findings about three-dimensional spindle skews using uncompressed embryos. The measurements are supported by Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, with appropriate controls showing no skew in P1 cells. The discovery of the LR-DV plane skew represents an important extension of previous work.

results.result: Cell fate determines both the presence of chiral counter-rotating flows and spindle skew characteristics. Anteriorizing embryos via par-2; chin-1; lgl-1 (RNAi) results in both cell divisions exhibiting chiral flows, while posteriorizing via par-6 (RNAi) eliminates chiral flows. Corresponding changes in spindle skew angles occur in both compressed and uncompressed embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 present cell fate manipulation experiments with clear quantitative outcomes shown in Figure 3B-H. The bidirectional manipulation (anteriorizing and posteriorizing) provides strong evidence for the causal relationship between cell fate and both chiral flows and spindle skews. The consistency across compressed and uncompressed conditions strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Modulating chiral counter-rotating flow velocities through RhoA signaling perturbations (ect-2 and rga-3 RNAi) results in corresponding changes in spindle skew rates without affecting spindle elongation dynamics or overall contractility. This demonstrates that chiral flows mechanically drive spindle skews.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C102 present a critical test of the hypothesis that chiral flows drive spindle skews. The experimental design is strong: perturbations specifically affect chiral flows (C96) without changing contractility (Figure 4C) or spindle elongation rates (C99, Figure 4D), and skew rates change proportionally with flow velocities. This provides compelling evidence for the mechanical driving hypothesis (C102).

results.result: LIN-5/GPR-1/2 spindle orientation pathway perturbations do not prevent spindle skews in AB cells or P1 cells, indicating this pathway does not play an important role in driving spindle skews. Instead, the LIN-5/GPR-1/2 pathway determines initial spindle orientation while chiral actomyosin flows drive anaphase spindle skews.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 address the alternative hypothesis that the known spindle orientation pathway drives skews. The experimental evidence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) shows that despite spindle misalignment, substantial skews still occur upon lin-5 depletion, and P1 skews remain unchanged. This supports the conclusion that the two pathways have distinct roles (C109).

results.result: Temperature-sensitive nmy-2 mutants at restrictive temperature show complete loss of cytokinetic ring ingression but unchanged spindle elongation dynamics, while spindle skew rates are significantly reduced (0.33 ± 0.09°/min vs 1.43 ± 0.13°/min in controls). This demonstrates that functional actomyosin cortex with chiral flows is required for spindle skews across all AB lineage divisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C116 present the most direct test of the requirement for actomyosin in spindle skews using temperature-sensitive mutants. The experimental design is strong: complete loss of myosin function (C110) eliminates skews (C112) without affecting spindle elongation (C111), definitively ruling out the spindle elongation hypothesis. The systematic analysis across 11 divisions (C115, Figure 5C) demonstrates generality.

results.result: The direction of cell division skews is determined by chiral flow handedness and friction force distribution. AB cells skew in both AP-DV and LR-DV planes, with left-right asymmetric friction forces inferred from significantly increased y-direction flows on the left side compared to the right side of the AB cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C123 present a physical mechanism for skew directionality based on the bulldozer analogy. The key experimental evidence is the measured left-right asymmetry in flow velocities (C122, Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which is consistent with the hypothesis of asymmetric friction forces (C123). The logic connecting flow asymmetry to friction asymmetry is sound.

results.result: A quantitative physical model incorporating measured flow velocities, contact surface areas, and estimated friction coefficients successfully predicts experimentally measured spindle skew rates for wild type, ect-2 (RNAi), and rga-3 (RNAi) conditions. Left-right asymmetric ring ingression likely contributes to asymmetric contact surface areas (reduced on left side).
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C131 present quantitative validation of the physical model. The agreement between calculated and measured skew velocities (C124, Appendix 1—table 3) across multiple conditions is impressive. While the authors acknowledge the measurements are coarse approximations (C130), the quantitative agreement supports the proposed mechanism. The hypothesis about asymmetric ring ingression (C126-C128) is supported by measured surface area differences (C129).

results.result: Different embryo mounting methods result in different degrees of compression: agarose pad mounting compresses embryos (aspect ratio 1.29 ± 0.14), low-melt agarose reduces compression (aspect ratio 1.02 ± 0.3), and in-utero measurements show intermediate compression (aspect ratio 1.16 ± 0.7).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 present methodological characterization of embryo compression with quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The inference that in-utero compression is intermediate (C30) is reasonable based on the measured aspect ratios. This is important methodological information for interpreting the results.

results.result: Lineage-specific chiral flows of the actomyosin cortex drive lineage-specific cell rearrangements in early C. elegans development, with the actomyosin cortex driving active counter-rotation of dividing AB lineage cell halves during anaphase. This represents a general mechanism for cell repositioning during division.
results.evaluation: Claims C135, C137, and C138 represent the main conclusions of the study. C135 and C137 are well-supported by the extensive experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript. However, C138's claim that this is a "general mechanism" is more speculative, as it extends beyond the C. elegans system studied. The evidence strongly supports the mechanism in C. elegans but generality to other systems remains to be tested.

results.result: During early C. elegans development, cell lineage specifications are driven by short-range intercellular signaling, making correct cell positioning instrumental for normal development. Chiral flow-driven spindle skews allow AB lineage cells to acquire precise positions that permit normal cell fate inductions through mechanisms like Notch signaling and left-right patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 are well-supported by citations to published literature establishing the importance of cell positioning and short-range signaling in C. elegans development. Claim C144 is a reasonable hypothesis connecting the observed chiral flows to developmental outcomes, though it represents a proposed mechanism rather than directly demonstrated causality in this study.

results.result: The occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on symmetric cell division characteristics (cortical myosin distribution and cytokinetic ring position), which are controlled by cell lineage determinants like PAR proteins that modulate molecular motor distribution along the cell division axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 synthesize the mechanistic understanding from the experimental results. C145 and C146 are well-supported by the data presented in the study. C147 is a reasonable inference based on the par-2 experiments and cited literature, though the specific molecular mechanisms by which PAR proteins control chiral flows remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Chiral active fluid theory, treating the cortex as a two-dimensional gel with liquid-like properties that generates active torques, can quantitatively recapitulate observed chiral flow behavior in dividing AB blastomeres when local torque density is assumed proportional to measured NMY-2 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C151 describe the theoretical framework and its validation. The quantitative agreement between theory and experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8 supports C151. However, the molecular basis for torque generation and flow handedness remains unclear (C152), representing an important gap in understanding.

results.result: The molecular underpinnings determining flow handedness remain elusive. Multiple actin-binding proteins localize similarly to myosin and affect flow chirality. Both myosins and formins can twist actin filaments due to actin's helical nature, making them potential sources of molecular torques, and both are required for various cellular and organismal chiral processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 acknowledge limitations in molecular understanding while presenting reasonable hypotheses. C152 appropriately identifies a gap in knowledge. C153-C154 are supported by citations. C155-C157 present mechanistic possibilities based on cited literature about myosin and formin properties. C158 provides broader context. This represents honest assessment of what is and isn't understood.

results.result: The handedness of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows, together with asymmetries in effective friction forces between cells and surroundings, determine the direction of three-dimensional cell division skews. Friction force differences exist between the AB blastomere and egg shell on left and right sides, causing clockwise skew in the AP-DV plane and establishing the dorsoventral axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C163 present the integrated physical mechanism for three-dimensional skew directionality. C159 and C160 are well-supported by the experimental observations of skews in multiple planes. C162 is supported by the measured flow asymmetries. C163 represents a reasonable inference from the physical model, though direct measurement of friction forces is not provided.

results.result: Chiral rotatory movements of the actomyosin cortex are more prevalent in development than previously suspected. The cells of the early embryo represent a new class of active chiral material requiring explicit treatment of angular momentum conservation, and cell skews driven by actomyosin torque generation represent a novel class of lineage-specific morphogenetic rearrangements.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 present broader implications of the work. C132 is supported by the systematic observation of chiral flows across multiple divisions. C133 and C134 represent reasonable interpretations of the physical and biological significance, respectively, though they extend somewhat beyond the direct experimental evidence to propose broader conceptual frameworks.
